bluf.text: Eat vegetables and fruit at most meals. Five portions, or about 400 g a day, is the common target.
Build a meal from a staple, a main and a side, mostly from plants, with fish once or twice a week.
Make water or unsweetened tea your default drink.
Keep sweets, salty snacks and sugary drinks occasional, and serve them on a plate instead of eating from the package.
Eat regular meals, slowly, and with other people when you can.

paragraphs.text: Japan, South Korea, China, Germany and the World Health Organization all put plants at the centre. The WHO asks for at least 400 g of fruit and vegetables a day, Germany for at least five portions, and China for 300 to 500 g of vegetables plus 200 to 350 g of fruit.

The WHO, China and Korea all limit salt, sugar and fat. The WHO and China both set salt under 5 g a day and added or free sugar under about 50 g, and Korea tells people to choose foods lower in salt, sugar and fat.
Water is the default drink everywhere: about 1.5 litres a day in Germany, 1,500 to 1,700 ml in China, plain water over sugary drinks in Korea, and water or tea in Japan.

Fish is in, and red and processed meat is limited. Germany suggests fish once or twice a week and no more than 300 g of meat and sausage a week. China suggests 300 to 500 g of fish a week. Japan asks for a mix of vegetables, beans and fish.

They also advise on how to eat, not only what. Korea says not to skip breakfast, to avoid overeating and to eat with family often. Germany says to eat slowly and enjoy it. Japan says to enjoy meals at regular hours, and China to keep three regular meals.
Japan builds the day on grain dishes such as rice, with vegetable dishes next and fish, egg and meat dishes after that. Its guide describes meals as a staple, a main and side dishes.

Germany leans furthest toward plants, adding legumes at least weekly, a small handful of nuts daily and whole grains. China is the most specific on variety, asking for 12 different foods a day and 25 a week.
Every one of these food guides also includes physical activity. Japan draws a runner on top of its guide, and China names about 6,000 steps a day.

In Japan, 79,594 adults were followed for about 15 years. Those who followed the national food guide most closely had a 15% lower death rate than those who followed it least. This is an observational study, so it shows a link and not a cause.

Across 185 prospective studies and 58 trials, people who ate the most fibre had 15 to 30% lower rates of death, heart disease, stroke, type 2 diabetes and colorectal cancer than those who ate the least. The benefit was greatest at 25 to 29 g a day.
People eat more when the portion, package or plate is larger. A Cochrane review of 58 studies found a small to moderate effect, stronger in adults.
In a year-long trial of 97 women, the group told to add water-rich fruit and vegetables lost more weight than the group told only to cut fat, and reported less hunger.
Higher-protein meals are modestly more filling. One review suggests 1.2 to 1.6 g of protein per kg of body weight a day, with 25 to 30 g at a meal, and notes that long-term results are mixed.
The guideline targets describe a healthy pattern over weeks: at least 400 g of fruit and vegetables and 25 g of fibre a day, and under 5 g of salt. Nobody is expected to hit them at every meal.

A country's good health has many causes besides its food: healthcare, income, how much people walk, smoking and drinking. These guidelines show what several health authorities agree on. They do not prove that diet alone explains why people in those countries live long.

sections.heading: Fibre, whole grains and beans in practice

paragraphs.text: Fibre targets differ by country. The UK asks adults for 30 g a day; they average about 20 g. Japan's 2020 reference intakes set 21 g for men aged 18 to 64 and 18 g for women. China asks that 50 to 150 g of daily cereals be whole grains and mixed beans.

The health evidence on grains concerns whole grains. In 45 prospective studies, each extra 90 g a day, about two slices of wholegrain bread and a bowl of cereal, was linked to 19% less coronary heart disease and a 17% lower death rate. Refined grains showed little link. Germany's guide adds that whole grains keep people full longer.

Beans, lentils and chickpeas are filling. In nine short feeding trials, meals with them were rated 31% more filling, though people ate no less at the next meal. In 21 trials with 940 people, about one serving a day brought 0.34 kg more weight loss over six weeks. The NHS suggests adding them to stews, curries and salads.

Muscle responds to protein meal by meal. In a week-long study of eight adults, about 30 g at each of three meals raised 24-hour muscle protein building by 25% over the same total eaten mostly at dinner. A later review called the wider evidence on spreading protein limited and inconsistent.

Total protein has clearer support. Across 49 trials with 1,863 people doing resistance training, extra protein added about 0.3 kg of lean mass, with no further gain above about 1.6 g per kg of body weight daily. The effect was larger in trained lifters and smaller with age. A protein food at each meal covers both points without counting.

Ultra-processed is a category from the NOVA system, which sorts foods by processing. A product counts if its ingredient list includes substances rarely used in home kitchens, such as hydrogenated oils, or additives that make it more appealing, such as flavours, colours, emulsifiers and sweeteners.

Large observational studies link ultra-processed food with worse health. An umbrella review of 45 pooled analyses, covering about 9.9 million people, found higher intake associated with 32 outcomes, including a 21% higher death rate. It rated 41 of the 45 analyses as low or very low quality.

Trials point the same way but leave the reason open. A 2026 review of ten trials found more weight gain and faster eating on ultra-processed diets, but people ate more only when those diets were denser in energy, with low certainty. In an English trial of 55 adults, with both diets following national guidelines, the less processed one brought about twice the weight loss.

Scientists disagree on whether processing itself is the problem. The UK's scientific advisers called the links concerning in 2023 but urged caution, citing possible confounding and overlap with existing advice. A published debate agreed that processing affects health but split on whether the NOVA label adds anything beyond nutrients.

Sugary drinks are linked to weight gain in cohorts and trials. In cohorts of 174,252 adults, each extra daily serving went with 0.12 to 0.22 kg more gain a year; in trials, adults given sugary drinks gained 0.85 kg. In 17 cohorts, a daily serving was linked to 13% more type 2 diabetes after allowing for body fat.

Diet drinks and juice are not simple swaps. The WHO advised in 2023 against non-sugar sweeteners for weight control, finding no long-term benefit for body fat; the advice excludes people with diabetes. The NHS limits juice and smoothies to 150 ml a day combined. Germany's guide does not recommend sugar-sweetened or alcoholic drinks.

Several health authorities decline to name a safe amount of alcohol. The WHO's European office said in 2023 that no amount is free of health effects; the German Nutrition Society said in 2024 that none is health-promoting and safe. China calls alcohol no basic part of a daily diet, and Korea advises restraint.

Eating more slowly reduces how much is eaten at that meal. Across 22 experiments, slower eating led to lower intake with no extra hunger up to three and a half hours later. In 23 observational studies, fast eaters had a body mass index 1.78 units higher and about twice the odds of obesity.

Eating while distracted leads to eating more, both then and later. A review of 24 experiments found a moderate increase during the distracted meal and a larger one at the next. Recalling a recent meal lowered later intake. Meals eaten away from the screen use both findings.

Eating with friends is not a way to eat less. A review of 42 studies found strong evidence that people eat more with friends than alone, with no such effect among strangers. Germany's guide still calls eating in company beneficial, so shared meals have value, just not for eating less.

Distance matters as well as portion size. A Cochrane review found that food placed farther away was eaten less, a moderate effect across 12 studies with 1,098 people, though certainty was low and most tests were lab-based. Snacks kept in a cupboard away from the desk apply the idea.

Breakfast is not a proven weight-loss tool. In 13 randomised trials, people assigned breakfast ate more over the day than those assigned to skip it, and ended 0.44 kg heavier. The trials were short and at risk of bias. Whether to eat breakfast can reasonably follow appetite and routine.

Eating the same food later made people hungrier in one controlled trial. Sixteen adults with overweight or obesity ate identical meals on two schedules, the later one shifted about four hours and ending two and a half hours before bed. It doubled the odds of hunger and lowered energy used while awake. The study was small and short.

Longer trials suggest a small benefit from eating earlier in the day. A review of 29 trials with 2,485 people, each at least 12 weeks long, found about 1.75 kg more weight loss when more food came earlier in the day. The authors called the effects small and uncertain, with high risk of bias in 22 trials.

Some patterns of overeating call for professional help. The NHS describes binge eating disorder as regularly eating a lot of food in a short time until uncomfortably full, often alone or in secret, with guilt or shame afterwards. It advises seeing a doctor as soon as possible if this sounds familiar.

sections.heading: Eating patterns that have been tested

paragraphs.text: The Mediterranean diet has been tested in a large randomised trial. In Spain, 7,447 adults aged 55 to 80 at high cardiovascular risk were followed for a median of 4.8 years. Heart attack, stroke or cardiovascular death struck 3.8% and 3.4% of the olive oil and nut groups, against 4.4% on low-fat advice. A Cochrane review found little or no effect on total deaths.

Nordic and Japanese patterns rest mainly on observational studies. In 15 cohorts with over a million people, the closest followers of a Nordic pattern had 7% less cardiovascular disease, with low certainty. Nine studies linked a Japanese-style diet to 17% lower cardiovascular death rates, though most measured diets in the 1980s and 1990s.

Studies that ask people what they ate get answers that run low. In five US studies checked against biological markers, people under-reported energy intake by 28% on food questionnaires and 15% on a one-day recall, more so at higher body mass index. Even defenders of these methods warn against treating it as true intake.

Falling short of the guidelines is normal, even in countries known for their food. Japan's health plan aimed for 350 g of vegetables a day, against an average of 282 g, and for 80% of people to eat a staple, main and side dish more than twice a day, against 68.1%. In Korea, the share eating 500 g of fruit and vegetables a day has fallen since 2015.

bluf.text: On a flat day, do ten easy minutes of movement instead of waiting to feel energetic first.
Break up long sitting with a few minutes of walking each hour.
Protect seven or more hours of sleep a night.
If tiredness lasts for weeks despite sleep and movement, tell a doctor, and mention your mood.

paragraphs.text: Across 81 randomised trials with 7,050 people, regular exercise reduced feelings of fatigue and raised feelings of energy and vitality. The effects were small to moderate.

In a six-week trial of 36 sedentary young adults with persistent fatigue, low-intensity exercise gave the better result for fatigue, and the gains did not depend on getting fitter. The trial was small.
In a trial of 30 sedentary adults, a five-minute walk every hour raised energy, improved mood and reduced fatigue and food cravings compared with six hours of unbroken sitting.
Exercise is also an effective treatment for depression, according to a review of 218 trials that rated its own confidence in the result as low. Walking or jogging and strength training both helped.
Feeling tired is common. In 2024, three in ten US adults slept less than seven hours a night, which is below what sleep specialists recommend.
Tiredness is rarely a sign of serious illness. Among people who saw a family doctor for it, 4.3% had a serious physical disease and 2.8% had anaemia, while 18.5% had depression.
The WHO guideline says some physical activity is better than none and that sitting time should be reduced.

A single bout of exercise changes several brain chemicals linked to mood and alertness. One review reports rises in dopamine, norepinephrine, endorphins and endocannabinoids, mostly measured in blood rather than in the brain. In a small trial of 20 tired women, blocking histamine in the brain made mental fatigue rise after light cycling, which did not happen without the drug.

Active adults are less likely to report low energy, but the reason is not settled. Across 12 population studies, active adults had 39% lower odds of low energy or fatigue than sedentary peers. The author found no compelling evidence for any biological mechanism, and such studies cannot show cause.

Pooled trials suggest regular exercise lifts energy on average, though expectation may explain part of it. A 2006 analysis found an average effect of 0.37 in favour of exercise. Trials that compared exercise alone with a placebo condition found no effect, so how much comes from the exercise itself remains uncertain.

sections.heading: Tired is not the same as sleepy

paragraphs.text: Sleepiness and fatigue are related but separate states, even though both are often just called tired. A 2006 review describes sleepiness as a change in the normal arousal system, the pull toward falling asleep. Fatigue has several definitions, and there is still no gold-standard way to measure it.

A dip in alertness in the mid-afternoon is normal and has roots in the body clock. A review describes this post-lunch dip as real even when no lunch is eaten and the person does not know the time. A high-carbohydrate lunch makes it worse, and it may be stronger in extreme morning types.

A short daytime nap can sharpen thinking for the next couple of hours. In a pooled analysis of 11 studies with 381 adults, napping improved mental performance, especially alertness, mainly for up to 120 minutes afterwards. Naps before 1 pm looked better, but that result was uncertain. Almost all studies were done in laboratories.

Long daily sitting is linked to a higher risk of early death, mainly in people who are not very active. In data on over 1 million adults, the least active people who sat over 8 hours a day had 59% higher death rates than active people who sat little. About 60 to 75 minutes of moderate activity a day seemed to remove the extra risk. Another review put the threshold at 6 to 8 hours.

Breaking up sitting with short bouts of activity improves how the body handles a meal. Across 37 trials, activity breaks moderately lowered blood sugar and insulin after eating, compared with unbroken sitting. The effect on blood sugar was larger in people with a higher body mass index, and blood fats fell slightly.

Changing the desk setup can cut sitting time, though the evidence is of low quality. A Cochrane review found sit-stand desks reduced sitting at work by about 100 minutes a day over the first three months. In one study, breaks of one to two minutes every half hour cut sitting by 40 minutes a day.

Light is the strongest signal for the body clock, which times sleepiness and alertness. A small brain area called the suprachiasmatic nucleus sets the release of melatonin, a sleep hormone, by how much light the eyes receive. Japan's 2023 sleep guide advises plenty of bright light by day and as little bright light as possible before bed.

People who spend more daylight hours outdoors report less tiredness. In a UK study of over 400,000 adults, each extra daily hour outdoors was linked to less frequent tiredness, easier getting up and fewer insomnia symptoms. Follow-up data pointed the same way with smaller effects. This shows a link, not a cause.

Bright light during the day can raise alertness within the same session. A systematic review of 62 experiments in healthy adults found that alertness and working memory were the outcomes most affected, and self-rated alertness improved most with bright white light. The light set-ups varied widely, so the best amount is unclear.

sections.heading: Caffeine lasts longer than it feels

paragraphs.text: Caffeine raises alertness, but its effect on sleep can last into the night. The European Food Safety Authority notes that a single 100 mg dose may affect sleep in some adults, mainly close to bedtime. Japan's sleep guide puts its half-life, the time for blood levels to halve, at 3 to 7 hours in Japanese people.

Pooled studies show that caffeine shortens sleep and makes it lighter. Across 24 studies, caffeine cut total sleep by 45 minutes and deep sleep by about 11 minutes. To avoid losing sleep, the authors advise having a 107 mg coffee at least 8.8 hours before bed, and a 217.5 mg dose at least 13.2 hours before.

Even caffeine taken 6 hours before bed can disturb sleep. In a home-based trial, 400 mg of caffeine taken at bedtime, 3 hours before or 6 hours before each disturbed sleep compared with a placebo. The authors concluded this supports avoiding large amounts for at least 6 hours before bed.

Losing water through sweat can dull attention, especially beyond about 2% of body weight. A pooled analysis of 33 studies with 413 people found a small overall drop in mental performance. Tasks of attention, coordination and planning were hit most, and the effect was larger when water loss exceeded 2% of body mass.

Mild water loss can also make people feel more tired. In two small trials, 26 men and 25 women lost about 1.4 to 1.6% of body weight through exercise and reported more fatigue, and the women also reported lower vigor and headaches. In another small study, people who usually drank little reported less fatigue after drinking more.

The rule of eight glasses of water a day has no direct study behind it. A 2002 review found no scientific studies supporting it for healthy adults in a mild climate, and noted that caffeinated drinks can count toward the total. More fluid is called for during hard work and exercise, especially in heat.

Fatigue and lack of energy are listed symptoms of depression, so the two can be hard to tell apart. The US National Institute of Mental Health says a diagnosis needs symptoms most of the day, nearly every day, for at least 2 weeks, including low mood or a loss of interest in most activities.

Tiredness and low mood often occur together. In a community study of about 2,600 Australian twins over 50, people with either fatigue or depression were about twice as likely to have both. Fatigue with poor sleep and poor concentration stood out as a warning sign of depression in this older group.

About one in five adults worldwide reports fatigue at any given time. A pooled analysis of 91 studies with over 620,000 people found general fatigue in 20.4% of adults and fatigue lasting more than 6 months in 10.1%. Women reported fatigue more often than men across every subgroup analysed.

In one large German survey, age showed no steady pattern in fatigue. Among 2,411 adults chosen to represent the population, women reported more physical, emotional and mental fatigue than men, and there were no linear age trends. The differences between women and men were small in size.

sections.heading: When to raise it with a doctor

paragraphs.text: Tiredness that lasts a few weeks without a clear reason is worth raising with a GP. The NHS also advises seeing one if tiredness affects daily life, comes with weight loss or mood changes, or if someone has noticed gasping, snorting or choking noises during sleep, which can be a sign of sleep apnoea.

A doctor usually starts with questions and an examination, then a few simple blood tests. A German family medicine review lists blood sugar, a blood count, an inflammation marker, liver enzymes and a thyroid test, plus iron stores in premenopausal women. Sleep problems, depression and heavy stress are the commonest causes it reports.

bluf.text: Treat the day after a short night as a day you will be hungrier, and decide what you will eat in advance.
Keep a steady wake time and aim for seven hours or more.
Put evening snacks on a plate or in a bowl and put the package away.
Make less-processed food the easy option at home, and fill up on fruit and vegetables first.

paragraphs.text: After a short night people eat more. Pooled sleep-restriction experiments found about 385 kcal more eaten the next day, with no increase in energy burned.

The kind of food matters. In a tightly controlled trial, 20 adults ate about 508 kcal a day more on an ultra-processed diet than on an unprocessed one, even though the meals offered were matched for calories, sugar, fat and fibre. They gained 0.9 kg in two weeks on one diet and lost 0.9 kg on the other.
The container matters too. Larger portions, packages and plates lead people to eat more, according to a Cochrane review of 58 studies.
Foods with a lot of water and fibre fill you up for less. In a year-long trial, women who added fruit and vegetables reported less hunger than women who only cut fat.
Sleep specialists recommend seven or more hours a night for adults. Three in ten US adults get less.
Eating more after a short night, or from a larger package, is what these experiments found on average. It is a common response to the situation, and the situation is the part you can change.

sections.heading: How a short night changes hunger

paragraphs.text: Short sleep raises hunger and food intake fairly consistently, while hormone changes are less consistent. Across 41 randomised trials, restricted sleep raised hunger ratings and led people to eat about 253 more calories a day. The review found no strong evidence that average levels of the appetite hormones leptin or ghrelin changed.

Other pooled studies point the same way, with a small rise in ghrelin, a hormone that drives hunger. A review of 21 studies with 2,250 people found slightly higher ghrelin in short sleepers. Another analysis found that sleeping 5.5 hours or less raised daily intake by about 204 calories.

Short sleep may also change which foods appeal. In a study of 12 young men, two short nights raised hunger by 24% and appetite for calorie-dense, high-carbohydrate foods by 33 to 45%. In a brain-imaging study, sleep loss dulled frontal areas that weigh food choices and raised desire for high-calorie foods.

sections.heading: Why the extra eating comes late

paragraphs.text: After short nights, much of the extra food tends to be eaten after dinner. In an inpatient study of 16 adults, five short nights raised energy burned by about 5%, but intake rose by more, especially at night after dinner. Weight rose about 0.8 kg, and the women showed less dietary restraint.

Sleeping longer reduced intake in a trial of people who usually slept too little. Among 80 adults with overweight who slept under 6.5 hours a night, one counselling session added about 1.2 hours of sleep. That group then ate about 270 fewer calories a day than the control group.

Going to bed and getting up at consistent times may matter as much as total sleep. In 60,977 UK adults tracked by wrist devices, the more regular sleepers had a 20 to 48% lower risk of death. Regularity predicted risk better than sleep length. The study was observational.

A US expert panel agreed that regular sleep timing is important for health, safety and performance. The panel, convened by the National Sleep Foundation, reviewed 63 publications. It judged weekend catch-up sleep may help when weekday sleep is short, but in one small trial, lie-ins did not stop extra eating after dinner.

A gap between the body clock and the hours that work demands is linked to higher body weight. In a large population study, this social jetlag was linked to a higher body mass index, beyond the effect of sleep length. It shows a link, not a cause.

A bright screen in the evening can push the body clock later. In a controlled study, reading on a light-emitting e-reader before bed instead of a printed book meant taking longer to fall asleep, less melatonin, a later body clock and lower alertness the next morning.

Experts agree more firmly about screens and sleep in young people than in adults. A National Sleep Foundation panel of 16 experts agreed that screen use impairs sleep in children and adolescents. It agreed on only 5 of 10 statements, and judged that changing screen habits may reduce the harm.

Blue-light-filtering glasses have not been shown to improve sleep. A Cochrane review of 17 small trials found mixed results for sleep quality and rated the evidence very low in certainty. The data were too uneven to pool, and the authors called for better trials.

Eating the same food later in the day raised hunger in a tightly controlled trial. Adults with overweight ate identical meals on early and late schedules. The late schedule increased hunger, raised the ratio of ghrelin to the fullness hormone leptin, and lowered energy burned while awake.

Eating more of the day's food earlier helped weight loss a little in short trials. A pooled analysis of 9 randomised trials found that, within a reduced-calorie diet, an earlier pattern led to about 1.2 kg more weight loss. The authors describe this as short-term and call for more studies.

The research does not show that any food after a set hour is harmful. In a Spanish observational study of 420 dieters, late main-meal eaters lost less weight despite similar intake. A review found harm mainly with large meals in people eating most of their food at night, while snacks of about 150 calories did not appear harmful.

Even two drinks in the evening can disturb dream sleep. A pooled analysis of 27 studies found that about two standard drinks reduced REM sleep, the dreaming stage, and more alcohol made it worse. Falling asleep faster was seen only after about five drinks.

Alcohol can help people drop off, but sleep later in the night suffers. A review of studies in healthy volunteers found more broken sleep in the second half of the night at all doses. Japan's sleep guide advises against heavy drinking and nightcaps, and suggests seeing a doctor if sleep seems to need one.

Stress tends to tilt eating toward less healthy food, though the effect is small. Across 54 studies with nearly 120,000 adults, a pooled analysis linked stress to slightly more eating overall, more unhealthy food and less healthy food. Stress also tops the NHS list of common causes of insomnia, alongside anxiety and depression.

Eating while distracted, for example at a screen, raises intake at that meal and later. Across 24 studies, distraction moderately increased how much was eaten at the time, and later intake even more. Not being able to see how much had been eaten also raised intake.

Snacks placed farther away get eaten less. A Cochrane review found such food was eaten moderately less, across 12 studies with 1,098 people, and the effect grew with distance. Certainty was low, and most studies were laboratory tests. Keeping snacks in the kitchen, not on the desk, applies this idea.

Binge eating disorder is a specific condition, different from sometimes eating more than planned. A US health institute describes a binge as a large amount of food in a short time, for example within 2 hours, with a feeling of lost control. Binges at least once a week for 3 months may point to the disorder.

Binge eating disorder also tends to involve eating very fast, past fullness and alone. Other signs are eating large amounts when not hungry, hiding it from embarrassment, and feeling disgusted, depressed or guilty afterwards. Unlike in bulimia, binges are not regularly followed by vomiting, laxatives, fasting or hard exercise.

Binge eating disorder is uncommon, although it is the most common eating disorder in the US. A survey of 36,306 US adults found it in 0.44% over the past year and 0.85% at some point in life, more often in women. Binges too infrequent to meet the criteria are much more common.

Anyone who thinks they may have binge eating disorder should see a GP soon, and effective treatment exists. The NHS reports that recovery is common with the right support, mainly guided self-help or cognitive behavioural therapy. Across 81 trials, psychotherapy, mostly of this kind, had large effects on binge episodes.

For long-term insomnia, US and European guidelines recommend cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia as the first treatment. It combines parts such as stimulus control, sleep restriction, relaxation and work on thoughts about sleep. Across 20 trials, it helped people fall asleep about 19 minutes faster and spend 26 fewer minutes awake.

Lists of sleep hygiene tips are a weak treatment on their own. The American Academy of Sleep Medicine advises against using sleep hygiene as a stand-alone therapy for insomnia, and 15 pooled studies found it less effective than cognitive behavioural therapy. The direct effect of single tips is largely untested.

The popular advice to avoid all evening exercise is not supported by pooled studies. Across 23 studies, evening exercise did not harm sleep, though vigorous exercise ending within an hour of bedtime might. In a separate analysis of 66 studies, regular exercise had small to moderate benefits for sleep.

bluf.text: Do some muscle-strengthening work twice a week. Thirty to sixty minutes in total is where the largest benefit was seen.
If twice is too much, do one short session. Beginners still get stronger.
Lift for strength and long-term health, and do not expect it to burn many calories.
If you are losing weight, keep lifting so that you lose fat and keep muscle.

paragraphs.text: Across 16 cohort studies, people who did muscle-strengthening activity had a 10 to 17% lower risk of early death, heart disease, cancer and diabetes. The largest reduction was at about 30 to 60 minutes a week. These are observational studies.

During weight loss, resistance training prevented about 93% of the muscle loss that dieting alone caused. The six trials were in older adults with obesity, so the size of the effect may differ for younger people.
Resistance training does not add to weight loss, but it may increase lean mass and fat loss and is associated with lower health risk.

A kilogram of muscle at rest uses about 13 kcal a day. Fat uses about 4.5, while the liver and brain use 200 or more per kilogram. Adding two kilograms of muscle therefore adds roughly 26 kcal a day at rest, so the popular idea that muscle burns a lot of calories passively is overstated.
The guideline for adults is muscle-strengthening activity on two days a week, alongside 150 minutes of moderate activity.

Beginners do not need much. One weekly session, with fewer than three sets per exercise and light loads, is enough to gain strength for at least the first 12 weeks. This comes from a narrative review, which is weaker evidence than a trial.

Skeletal muscle is the main tissue that clears sugar from the blood when insulin acts. In laboratory tests that hold insulin high, about 80 to 90% of the glucose given is taken up by muscle. Worked muscle also becomes more sensitive to insulin afterwards. Both points come from expert reviews.

More muscle relative to body size goes with better blood sugar control in a large US survey. Among 13,644 adults, each 10% rise in muscle relative to body weight was linked with 11% lower insulin resistance and 12% lower odds of prediabetes, after allowing for obesity. A single snapshot like this cannot show cause.

In people with type 2 diabetes, resistance training lowers HbA1c, a blood marker of average blood sugar over recent months. A review of 20 trials found a fall of 0.39 percentage points, and bigger strength gains went with bigger drops. An earlier review of 47 trials found resistance, aerobic and combined training each lowered HbA1c.

Sarcopenia is the medical name for the loss of muscle strength and mass that comes with age. A European expert group defines it as a muscle disease, with low strength as its key feature. The group notes that it is common in older age but can also begin earlier in life.

Strength fades faster than muscle size in later life. A review found that at about age 75, people lose roughly 0.6 to 1% of their muscle mass a year but 2.5 to 4% of their strength. Loss of strength was a more consistent risk for disability and death than loss of muscle.

Older muscles still respond well to training. Across 47 studies with 1,079 adults aged 50 and over, resistance training raised strength by about 24 to 33%, depending on the exercise tested, and harder training was linked with larger gains. The authors suggest training as a way to prevent the general weakness linked with ageing.

The bone built in youth sets the starting point for bone health later in life. A US National Osteoporosis Foundation statement says that lifestyle shapes 20 to 40% of adult peak bone mass. It found the best evidence for calcium and physical activity, especially in late childhood and around puberty. That is one reason starting early helps.

Resistance training can still add some bone density in later adulthood. In 17 studies of women after menopause, lifting raised spine and hip density by small to moderate amounts. In 14 trials in adults aged 65 and over, hip density rose about 2.8%, but the spine change was not significant.

Heavy lifting under supervision appeared safe for women with low bone mass in one Australian trial. In 101 women aged about 65, eight months of twice-weekly, 30-minute sessions at over 85% of maximum raised spine density by 2.9%, against a 1.2% loss with light home exercise. One minor adverse event, a lower back spasm, was reported.

Falls kill hundreds of thousands of people a year, mostly older adults. The World Health Organization estimated about 842,000 fall deaths in 2023, 71% of them in people aged 60 and over. It names weak strength and poor balance among the risks and advises exercise that challenges balance and builds functional strength.

Exercise programmes cut falls in older people, and the best-supported ones pair balance work with strength work. A Cochrane review of 108 trials with 23,407 people found exercise lowered the rate of falls by 23%. Mixed balance, functional and resistance programmes probably cut falls by 34%; resistance training alone had an uncertain effect.

sections.heading: Grip strength as a health signal

paragraphs.text: Grip strength, measured by squeezing a hand gauge, tracks with the risk of early death. In the PURE study of 139,691 adults in 17 countries, each 5 kg lower grip was linked with a 16% higher risk of death over about four years. Grip predicted death better than blood pressure but was not linked with falls or fractures.

Data from about 1.9 million adults point the same way. Across 38 cohort studies, higher grip strength was linked with a 31% lower risk of death, and stronger legs with a 14% lower risk. These are observational links, so they cannot show cause.

A strong grip may partly reflect body size and general health rather than training. In a Chinese cohort of 12,957 adults, grip relative to body weight predicted lower risk of type 2 diabetes, but grip in kilograms did not, and body fat helped explain the link. The PURE authors say it is still untested whether gaining strength lowers death rates.

Resistance training eased symptoms of depression in randomised trials. A review of 33 trials with 1,877 adults found a moderate reduction in depressive symptoms. The benefit did not depend on training volume or on whether people got significantly stronger. Trials with blinded assessment showed smaller benefits.

Lifting also eased anxiety a little in randomised trials. A review of 16 trials found a small drop in anxiety symptoms, larger in healthy people. A 2024 depression review found a benefit from strength training a little smaller than from walking or jogging, with very low confidence. Low mood that lasts for weeks calls for a doctor or therapist.

sections.heading: Back pain, joints and daily tasks

paragraphs.text: Exercise eased long-lasting low back pain in many trials. A Cochrane review of 249 trials found that exercise cut pain by about 15 points on a 100-point scale compared with no treatment or usual care, with moderate certainty. The gain in daily function was smaller. Side effects were mostly minor, such as soreness.

In older adults, strength training made everyday movements easier and eased arthritis pain. A Cochrane review of 121 trials with 6,700 people found a large gain in strength, a moderate to large improvement in getting up from a chair and a modest rise in walking speed. In six trials of people with osteoarthritis, joint pain fell.

sections.heading: How fast strength comes and goes

paragraphs.text: Much of the strength gained in the first weeks comes from the nervous system learning to use muscle better. A 2021 review states that early increases in force are thought to come mainly from changes in the nerves that drive muscle. Exactly where these changes happen is still unclear.

Strength fades when training stops, and it fades more the longer the break. A review of 103 studies found losses in all measures of strength and power after training stopped. The losses were larger in people over 65 and, for maximal strength and power, larger in inactive people than in recreational athletes.

Some of the gain survives a break, and it returns quickly. In a Belgian study of 30 older men, 12 weeks of training raised leg strength by 10 to 36%, 12 weeks off lost 5 to 15%, and under eight weeks of retraining restored it. A small Norwegian study found extra muscle cell nuclei persisted after 16 weeks off, with unclear benefit.

Women and men gain muscle and leg strength at similar rates when they train the same way. A review of up to 23 studies in young and middle-aged adults found similar relative gains in muscle size and lower-body strength, and larger relative upper-body strength gains in women. Short study lengths may partly explain that difference.

Japan's 2023 national activity guide advises muscle training on two to three days a week for adults and older people. For older people, it also advises activity that mixes several types of exercise on at least three days a week. The guide comes from Japan's health ministry and is summarised in a 2025 overview.

Most evidence linking strength with longer life comes from observational studies, which follow people over time. Such studies adjust for known differences between people but cannot rule out every other explanation. The PURE authors call for research on whether improving strength reduces deaths. The trials here show effects on strength, blood sugar, bone and mood, not lifespan.

bluf.text: To lose weight, change eating first. Use exercise to keep the weight off and to feel better.
Expect slow change. One to two pounds a week is the pace most likely to last.
Choose changes you could still be doing a year from now.
Treat BMI as a rough screen, not a verdict on your health.

paragraphs.text: In trials that compared them directly, programmes combining diet and activity beat activity-only programmes by about 6.3 kg after 12 to 18 months, and beat diet-only programmes by about 1.7 kg at 12 months. Most of the weight loss comes from the diet side.

The American College of Sports Medicine says 150 to 250 minutes of moderate activity a week prevents weight gain but produces only modest loss by itself, and that observational studies link more than 250 minutes to better weight maintenance, though no well-designed trial has tested it.
Exercise alone tends to produce a smaller energy deficit than the arithmetic predicts, partly because people eat a little more or move less for the rest of the day.
Extra muscle changes resting calorie burn only a little, because a kilogram of muscle uses about 13 kcal a day at rest.

About one in five people with overweight lose at least 10% of their weight and keep it off for a year. People in a US registry who have kept weight off for years report about an hour of activity a day, regular breakfast, weighing themselves, and eating the same way on weekends as on weekdays. They are a self-selected group, so these are habits they share and not proven causes.
Five years after a structured weight-loss programme, the average person had kept off about 3 kg.

For adults, a BMI of 18.5 to under 25 is classed as healthy weight, 25 to under 30 as overweight, and 30 or more as obesity. At 5 ft 9 in and 185 lb, BMI works out to about 27.3. The CDC calls BMI a screening measure to be considered with other factors.
People who lose about one to two pounds a week are more likely to keep it off, and even modest loss can improve blood pressure, cholesterol and blood sugar.
Regaining some weight is the usual outcome, as the five-year figure shows. It reflects how hard maintenance is for most people.

Hunger can stay raised long after a diet ends. In an Australian study, 50 adults with overweight or obesity lost an average of 13.5 kg (about 30 lb) over 10 weeks. A year later their appetite hormones had not returned to pre-diet levels, and they rated their hunger higher than before.

Appetite appears to push back harder than metabolism does. Researchers modelled a year-long trial of 153 people taking a drug that passes sugar out in urine, so they lost weight without sensing it. Their eating rose in step with the weight lost, by over three times the drop in energy burned. Extra hunger after weight loss is expected.

The idea of a permanently damaged metabolism is not well supported. A systematic review of 33 studies with 2,528 people found energy use often fell more than expected after weight loss. The drop was small or not significant in better-designed studies, and seemed to fade once weight had been stable for a while.

BMI cannot tell muscle from fat. The NHS says a muscular person may land in the overweight or obese range without much body fat. A Lancet commission of 58 experts advised in 2025 that BMI be used only for screening, with excess fat confirmed by a waist measure or a direct measure of body fat.

Waist size adds information that the scale cannot. The NHS advises keeping the waist to less than half of height, which at 5 ft 9 in means under 34.5 inches. The US National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute puts the risk line at 40 inches for men and 35 for women. Japanese criteria use 85 cm for men, about 33.5 inches.

Waist measured against height picks out health risk better than BMI does. In a meta-analysis of 31 papers covering more than 300,000 adults, waist-to-height ratio beat both BMI and waist size alone at identifying people with high blood pressure, type 2 diabetes and heart disease, in men and in women.

The BMI lines are not the same for everyone. For people of South Asian, Chinese, other Asian, Middle Eastern, Black African or African-Caribbean background, the NHS treats 23 as overweight and 27.5 as obese. A WHO expert group found a substantial share of Asian people at high risk of type 2 diabetes below a BMI of 25.

Being fit appears to offset much of the risk linked to a higher weight. A 2025 meta-analysis pooled 20 cohort studies that measured fitness on an exercise test. Fit people with overweight or obesity had no statistically different death rate from fit people of normal weight. Unfit people had roughly double the risk at every weight.

Exercise can change the body even when the scale does not move. Across 117 studies with 4,815 people, exercise without weight loss went with about 6% less visceral fat, the deep belly fat that predicts illness better than weight does. Diet without weight loss showed almost no change. A steady scale can hide real progress from training.

Weight still matters, modestly in the overweight range. Among 3.95 million never-smokers on four continents, death rates were lowest at a BMI of 20 to 25, about 7% higher at 25 to 27.5 and 20% higher at 27.5 to 30. In trials of weight loss in adults with obesity, deaths from any cause were 18% lower.

A plateau at about six months is the usual pattern in weight-loss trials. Across 80 trials with at least a year of follow-up, diet-based programmes, some with medicines, gave an average loss of 5 to 8.5 kg in six months, then levelled off. After four years, 3 to 6 kg stayed off. Across 49 trials, men lost slightly more than women, with little sign that the sexes need different approaches.

Losing weight slowly may not protect against regain as much as is often said. In an Australian trial of 204 adults with obesity, one group lost weight over 12 weeks and the other over 36 weeks. Three years later, both groups had regained about 71% of the loss. The trial does not show that faster loss is better either.

Sleeping longer reduced how much people ate in one trial, with no diet involved. Eighty adults with overweight who usually slept under 6.5 hours were randomised. Coaching added about 1.2 hours of sleep a night, and that group ate about 270 kcal a day less than the comparison group and lost weight relative to it.

Stress nudges eating and weight, but only slightly on average. A meta-analysis of 54 studies with 119,820 people linked stress to more unhealthy food and less healthy food. Across 14 long-term cohorts, stress went with gaining body fat, but the authors called the effect very small.

Eating late in the day may itself raise hunger. In a tightly controlled crossover trial of 16 adults with overweight or obesity, eating the same meals about four hours later doubled the odds of feeling hungry. The trial was small and short. Having a proper meal earlier in the evening is a low-cost thing to try.

Overeating that feels out of control is a reason to get professional help. The NHS describes binge eating disorder as regularly eating a lot of food in a short time until uncomfortably full, often alone or in secret, with guilt or shame afterwards. It advises seeing a GP as soon as possible if this sounds familiar.

Keeping weight off for years is possible, and it goes with keeping habits up. Among 2,886 people in the US National Weight Control Registry, mostly women, an average of 23 kg was still off after 10 years. Those who regained more had become less active. Members volunteer and self-report, so this shows links, not causes.

Registries in Europe point the same way. A review of 52 articles from registries in the US, Portugal, Germany, Finland and Greece found common habits such as keeping healthy food at home, regular breakfast and more vegetables. More activity was the most consistent link. In a review of 67 studies, demographics did not predict who kept weight off.

The evidence that yo-yo dieting harms metabolism is thin. A review of 31 human studies found that 13 of 17 showed no harmful effect of weight cycling on type 2 diabetes risk, and that findings on body fat and later weight gain were inconclusive. The authors concluded that efforts to lose weight should still be encouraged.

Large swings in weight are linked to worse outcomes, but cause is not shown. A meta-analysis of 23 cohort studies with 441,199 people found weight fluctuation associated with a 41% higher death rate. Observational studies like these cannot separate the swings from illness or other causes behind them, and there were signs of publication bias.

Shame about weight is linked to less healthy behaviour, not more. A review of 38 studies found weight teasing, everyday discrimination and self-directed stigma associated with less physical activity, though results were mixed. In a study of 6,157 older US adults, those who reported weight discrimination were about 2.5 times more likely to develop obesity over four years.

The NHS says losing weight can be hard and extra support or treatment may be needed. It suggests seeing a GP when BMI is overweight or obese and help is wanted. A GP can refer people to weight management programmes, medicines or surgery. Whether any fits is a decision to make with a doctor.

The World Health Organization calls obesity a chronic, relapsing disease. Its 2025 guideline says GLP-1 medicines may be used for long-term treatment of obesity in adults, defined as a BMI of 30 or more, alongside diet and activity support. The advice is conditional because long-term data are limited, and WHO says medicines alone will not solve the problem.

After a missed day, the only job is to do the next one.

Choose activity that feels good while you are doing it.

paragraphs.text: In a field experiment with 61,293 gym members and 54 different programmes, the best performer offered a small reward for coming back after a missed workout. It raised weekly visits by 27%.

Programmes that combined self-monitoring with another self-regulation step, such as setting a goal or reviewing progress, worked better than those that did not (an effect of 0.42 against 0.26 across 122 evaluations).
People who feel better during moderate exercise are more likely to be active later. How they feel after the session did not predict it.
Across 66 studies, doing exercise for your own reasons, because you enjoy or value it, was consistently linked to exercising more.

Habits take longer than the popular 21 days. In the studies that timed it, the middle person took 59 to 66 days, and individuals ranged from 4 to 335 days. Most of these studies were rated at high risk of bias.
Most nudges fade. In the gym experiment, only 8% of programmes still had a measurable effect after they ended.
Dropping a tracking app is the norm. In one food-photo app, 2.58% of about 190,000 users kept using it actively.
People who fit their weekly activity into one or two days had similar death rates to people who spread it across the week, in a study of 350,978 adults.

A habit is an action done almost daily in the same setting, and it runs with little thought. In two diary studies, people doing habitual actions tended to think about unrelated things. They also reported less stress than during actions that were new or done in changing settings.

Habit researchers advise repeating the same action in the same situation. A review written for family doctors suggests choosing a time and place met every day of the week, so the setting starts to prompt the action. This is expert guidance drawn from habit studies, not a trial result.

Exercising at a regular time of day was linked to doing more of it. Among 375 US adults who had kept off lost weight, 68% exercised mostly in the same time window. They reported more active days and more often met 150 minutes a week, 86% against 74%.

An if-then plan names when and where an action will happen, for example going straight to the gym after work on Monday. Across 13 randomised trials, adults who used such plans and had them reinforced over time became more active, with a small effect of 0.25.

A larger review of 41 trials with 5,439 people found that planning raised physical activity by a small amount, 0.35 on a standard scale. Plans worked better when they were made face to face and when they were reinforced during follow-up.

If-then plans also help with eating, more for adding foods than for cutting them. In 23 studies, plans to eat more of a healthy food had an effect of 0.51, against 0.29 for eating less unhealthy food. A review of 12 studies with 3,323 people found a moderate effect of 0.49 for cutting fat.

Habit researchers advise small, manageable changes, because failure can be discouraging. This is expert advice rather than a measured finding. A short walk after the same meal each day fits it better than a plan that needs a free hour.

A leaflet of simple habit tips produced modest weight loss in a UK trial of 537 adults with obesity. The Ten Top Tips group lost 0.87 kg more than usual care at 3 months. By 24 months the usual care group had lost a similar amount.

Programmes built to form exercise habits do strengthen them. In a meta-analysis of 10 studies, habit strength rose by a small amount, 0.31, and programmes that taught problem solving did better. Effects were larger at follow-ups of 12 weeks or less than at longer ones.

Self-efficacy means confidence in one's own ability to do something, and it can be raised. Across 27 studies with 5,501 healthy adults, programmes raised it by a small amount. Feedback on past performance, and watching others do the activity, gave the largest gains.

Some popular techniques were linked to lower confidence, not higher. Persuasion, graded steps and listing barriers went with lower self-efficacy in one review. In a second analysis, action planning, clear instruction and praise for effort went with higher confidence and more activity.

One missed day does not undo a habit that is forming. In the habit study described in a review for family doctors, the automatic pull of the action soon returned after a single missed performance. The review reports that missing the occasional opportunity did not seriously impair habit formation, so one gap is no reason to start over.

Confidence about getting back on track was linked to fewer lapses. In a Dutch study, 81 adults trying to lose weight answered six short prompts a day for two weeks. Higher confidence in recovering from a lapse went with lower odds of skipping exercise, while feeling hungry went with higher odds.

Treating oneself kindly after a setback is linked to healthier behaviour. A meta-analysis of 19 studies with 9,660 adults found a modest link between self-compassion and health-promoting behaviour, partly through lower stress. The studies measured links, so they cannot show cause and effect.

Placing food farther away reduces how much of it gets eaten. In a Cochrane review, 12 studies with 1,098 people found a moderate drop in eating when food was put farther from reach. The evidence was rated low certainty, and most studies took place in laboratories.

A common rule of thumb follows: put the wanted action within reach and the unwanted one out of the way. For late eating at a desk, that can mean keeping snacks in another room. For exercise, it can mean leaving the gym bag packed by the door. This is practical advice, not a tested finding.

Saving a favourite pleasure for exercise time raised gym visits at first. In a US field experiment, people who could hear gripping audiobooks only at the gym went 51% more often than controls early on. The effect faded over time, yet 61% later paid to keep the arrangement.

Cash rewards raise activity while they last, and some of the effect may remain. In 23 trials, about 1.40 US dollars a day added about 600 steps a day during programmes and about 500 afterwards. A 2025 update of 29 studies found a moderate effect during programmes, a small one afterwards and little long-term evidence.

Expected rewards can lower interest in an activity, while praise tends to raise it. A meta-analysis of 128 experiments found that tangible, expected rewards reduced later free-choice interest, and positive feedback increased it. The review covered motivation in general, not exercise in particular.

Exercising in a group did not clearly beat exercising alone. A 2026 meta-analysis of 71 studies found a small advantage for group programmes on physical activity, but it was not statistically significant. Both group and individual approaches, in person or online, may work.

Support from friends is linked to being more active. In 19 studies of college and university students, social support was moderately related to physical activity, and support from friends more strongly than support from family. These studies measured links, not effects.

The idea that willpower is a fuel that runs out did not hold up in a large replication. Across 23 laboratories and 2,141 people, the effect of one self-control task on the next was close to zero. The test used one standard pair of tasks, so it does not settle every version of the idea.

No single best time of day for exercise appeared in the registry study. Activity levels did not differ by the time people chose, as long as it stayed consistent. Early morning was common, chosen by 48% of the consistent exercisers.

Planning seems to help some people more than others. In the reviews, plans to cut fat worked better for men than for women, and activity plans worked better for men and for patients. A review of 24 studies concluded that if-then plans suit people who already intend to act and feel able to.

Research on keeping a change for years is thin. A review of 100 behaviour theories noted that programmes achieve temporary change but lasting change is rarely attained. A review of 15 long-term studies found habit and activity linked in both directions, so which comes first is still unclear.

bluf.text: If you have ever sprained an ankle, do balance work every week.
Practise soft, quiet landings before you add more jumping.
When climbing, build up slowly and use an open hand where you can instead of a hard crimp.
Treat falling as a skill. Most bouldering fall injuries are to the legs and ankles.

paragraphs.text: Ankle sprains are the commonest acute volleyball injury, and up to 80% happen to an ankle that was sprained before.

In a trial across 116 volleyball teams, balance-board training reduced ankle sprains, and the benefit was significant only for players who had sprained an ankle before. Players with a history of knee injury had more overuse knee problems on the programme.
Pooled across 17 studies, balance training cut the risk of an ankle sprain by about 40%, and by about half in people with a previous sprain. Ankle braces performed about as well.
For preventing a repeat sprain, an overview of 46 reviews found strong evidence for bracing and moderate evidence for balance and control training.
Volleyball injury reviews recommend landing technique and balance training as the main prevention measures.
Jump training does raise vertical jump in volleyball players, across 14 trials.

In climbers, overuse injuries were more likely with higher climbing intensity, bouldering, weak fingers or grip, the crimp grip and a previous injury. Body weight and BMI were not linked to injury. The 34 studies were of low average quality.
In a survey of 301 bouldering fall injuries, 67% were to the lower limb and the most common was an ankle sprain. In 85% of cases the fall was not intended.
Sore knees are common in volleyball. Jumper's knee affects about 40 to 50% of male indoor players, and shoulder pain accounts for 8 to 20% of injuries.

A common rule of thumb, not taken from these sources: muscle soreness for a day or two after something new is expected, while pain inside a joint that is still there the next morning is a reason to back off and have it looked at.

An International Olympic Committee expert group named poor load management as a major risk factor for injury in athletes. Load here covers rapid changes in training and competition, crowded schedules, psychological stress and travel. It was written for elite sport, not recreational play.

One influential review argues that hard training protects, and that sudden spikes are what cause harm. Its author wrote that excessive and rapid increases in load are likely behind a large share of non-contact soft-tissue injuries. He recommends building up to high loads in graded steps. This is a narrative review, so it proposes a model rather than testing one.

The acute-to-chronic workload ratio, which compares recent training with a longer-term average, became the best-known way to spot spikes. A 2020 critique found no evidence supporting its use for training decisions aimed at reducing injury. The authors added that the ratio is an inaccurate measure that adds statistical noise.

A 2026 meta-analysis of 16 studies with 797 team-sport athletes found a small-to-moderate link between a high acute-to-chronic ratio and injury. Results varied enormously from study to study. The authors concluded that the ratio should be read as one sign within a wider monitoring system, not as a stand-alone predictor of injury.

sections.heading: Warm-ups that train balance and landing

paragraphs.text: In football, a structured warm-up called the FIFA 11+ reduced injuries by 39% when four trials were pooled. An earlier routine, the FIFA 11, showed no effect in two trials, so not every warm-up works. The trials were in recreational and sub-elite players.

Short balance and strength sessions, two or three times a week, appear to be enough to lower leg injury risk. Pooling 16 trials in athletes aged 21 or under, one meta-analysis found 42% fewer leg injuries, and 10 to 15 minute sessions worked as well as longer ones. Another pooled analysis across youth team sports found a 36% reduction.

For female athletes, these programmes show their clearest benefit for the knee. A 2025 review of 82 studies in female athletes found that balance, strength and agility programmes done for at least 10 minutes twice a week cut ACL injuries, tears of the main ligament inside the knee, by 61% with high certainty. For all leg injuries the reduction was 19%, with low certainty.

Across 25 trials with 26,610 people, strength training showed the largest protective effect of any exercise type studied. It cut sports injuries to less than a third of the usual rate. Balance training reduced them by about 45%, programmes mixing several methods by about a third, and stretching made no difference.

A later review of six strength-training trials, with 7,738 people aged 12 to 40, again found injury risk cut to about a third. More training brought more protection: each 10% rise in strength-training volume lowered injury risk by more than four percentage points.

Stretching before exercise did not prevent injury in a large army trial. In Australia, 1,538 recruits either added a 20-second stretch for six leg muscle groups to every warm-up or did not, for 12 weeks. Injury rates were similar. Fitness and age predicted injury risk, while height, weight and BMI did not.

A 2026 review pooled 15 studies with more than 9,000 people and found no effect of regular stretching on muscle, tendon or ligament injuries. Certainty was very low, and most participants were men. No study tested whether stretching just before activity changes injury risk.

Tendons, the cords that join muscle to bone, respond slowly to exercise in adults. A review found adult tendon far less responsive to single bouts of loading than animal tendon. Losing load works faster: two to three weeks of leg immobilisation cut collagen production by about 80%.

Holding a muscle contraction without moving, called an isometric hold, can ease knee tendon pain for a while. In six volleyball players, one session of isometric contractions cut pain during a single-leg squat from about 7 to near 0 out of 10, for at least 45 minutes. A four-week trial in 20 athletes found holds gave more immediate relief than moving lifts.

For lasting relief from knee tendon pain, trials favour strength work that gets gradually heavier. In a Danish trial of 39 men with knee tendon pain, heavy slow lifting gave gains that held at six months, while steroid injections helped only briefly. In a Dutch trial of 76 patients, progressive tendon loading beat eccentric exercise at 24 weeks, yet only 43% were back in sport.

sections.heading: Soreness, pain and the next morning

paragraphs.text: Delayed muscle soreness is most common at the start of a season or after a new kind of exercise. Movements where the muscle lengthens under load cause more of it. A review advises easing off for a day or two after a hard session and bringing in new exercises over one or two weeks. Ice and stretching did not ease the soreness.

Some rehabilitation programmes use a pain-monitoring rule instead of complete rest. Pain may reach 5 out of 10 during or just after activity, but should settle to its usual level by the next morning. In a Swedish trial of 38 people with Achilles tendon pain, those who kept running and jumping under this rule improved as much as those who stopped.

In teenagers, chronic poor sleep goes with more sports injuries. A meta-analysis of seven studies found that adolescents who slept poorly over time had 58% higher odds of injury. The effect of a single bad night is not settled. These studies were observational, so they show a link and not a cause.

In adults, the evidence linking poor sleep to injury is limited. A review of 12 prospective cohort studies in adult athletes concluded that current evidence does not support poor sleep as an independent risk factor for injury. The authors called for better studies rather than ruling it out.

More training combined with less sleep may matter more than either alone. Among 496 Swedish elite athletes aged 15 to 19 followed for a year, those whose training load and intensity rose while their sleep fell had 2.25 times the injury risk, the strongest factor found. Separately, an expert panel recommends seven or more hours of sleep a night for adults.

sections.heading: Coming back from an ankle sprain

paragraphs.text: The NHS advises protection, rest, ice, compression and elevation for the first two to three days after a sprain, and avoiding heat, alcohol and massage. Most sprains feel better after two weeks. Strenuous exercise such as running may need to wait up to eight weeks, and severe sprains can take months.

For ankle sprains, a Dutch evidence-based guideline prefers supervised exercise to passive treatments, because exercise helps restore the ankle's stability. After a torn ankle ligament, a short spell of immobilisation may ease pain and swelling, but tape or a brace combined with exercise helps most. Surgery is kept for ankles that do not respond to thorough exercise treatment.

There were no guidelines for deciding when to play again after a sprain, so an international panel of 155 health professionals drew up a checklist. It covers pain during sport and over the past day, ankle movement and strength, confidence in the ankle, balance, and hopping, jumping, agility and finishing a full training session.

Some signs after an injury need emergency care. The NHS lists hearing a crack, a limb that has changed shape or points at an odd angle, and numbness, tingling or skin that turns blue, grey or cold. It advises urgent advice if the injury is very painful, swelling keeps growing, or no weight can be put on it.

Injuries that heal slowly also deserve a check. The NHS advises seeing a doctor if knee pain has not improved within a few weeks, or if a sprain is getting worse or not improving with self-care. In many areas of the UK, people can refer themselves to physiotherapy without seeing a doctor first.

bluf.text: Count every volleyball night toward the 150 to 300 minutes of weekly activity the WHO recommends.
Protect your ankles with weekly balance work, most of all if you have sprained one before.
For a higher jump, a small amount of jump training works. Keep it small, because volleyball is already a lot of jumping.
Take pain just below the kneecap seriously early. It is the sport's commonest overuse problem.

paragraphs.text: Health data on volleyball itself is thin. A large study of specific sports followed 80,306 British adults across six activities, and volleyball was not one of them. It found lower death rates among people who played racquet sports, swam, did aerobics or cycled, and no clear link for running or football.

What can be said is that volleyball counts as activity. The WHO guideline is 150 to 300 minutes of moderate or 75 to 150 minutes of vigorous activity a week, and three nights of play goes a long way toward it.
Across 14 randomised trials with 322 volleyball players, jump training improved vertical jump height.
Ankle sprains make up as much as half of volleyball injuries, and up to 80% involve an ankle that was sprained before. Balance-board training reduced them in a trial of 116 teams.
Across sports, balance training lowers ankle sprain risk by about 40%.
Knee and shoulder complaints are part of the sport for many players. About 40 to 50% of male indoor players have had jumper's knee.

sections.heading: How much jumping the game involves

paragraphs.text: Volleyball is a game of repeated jumps and landings. In video of elite women's matches, each player averaged nearly 22 jump-landings per game. Most jumps were taken off two feet, but more than half of the landings after a block were on one foot. The study covered only two matches among four teams.

Setters on one professional team averaged 121 jumps per training session. Sensors on 14 professional players recorded 129,173 jumps across 142 sessions in a season. Weekly totals swung widely, and every player had at least one week in which the jump count doubled.

In young elite players, more volleyball went with more jumper's knee. A four-year Norwegian study followed 141 players aged 16 to 18, and 28 developed it. Each extra weekly hour of training raised the odds about 1.7 times, and each extra set of matches per week about 3.9 times. Boys had three to four times the risk of girls, and body composition made no difference.

In adult professional players, a link between jump load and knee pain has not been confirmed. Tracking 65 elite men over three seasons and more than 21,000 sessions, a Norwegian study found no certain link between weekly jump load and knee complaints. Differences in risk were small, and the authors say much larger studies would be needed to settle the question.

How a player lands may matter for the knee tendon. In a Dutch laboratory study, players who had recovered from jumper's knee landed from drop jumps with stiffer knees and faster loading than healthy players. The authors suggest stiff landing may be a risk factor, though each group had only seven to nine players and the design cannot show cause.

Most ACL injuries in volleyball happen without contact, usually when landing from a spike. The ACL is the main ligament in the middle of the knee. A review of 15 studies found the highest rates in female high-school players and in outside hitters, with rates varying widely by exposure and level of play.

Shoulder pain is common among competitive volleyball players, though estimates depend on how it is defined. A 2026 review of 27 studies put its prevalence between 22% and 38%. Linked factors included earlier shoulder pain, poor control of the shoulder blade, strength imbalance and the number of arm swings. Most studies were observational and at risk of bias.

Hitters and jump servers report more shoulder trouble than other players. Among 422 US college club players, about 60% reported a past shoulder problem, and attackers and jump servers had more problems than setters, defensive players and float servers. Women reported more limitation than men. The study was a one-time survey and examination.

In volleyball, a trial of a shoulder warm-up measured fitness rather than injuries. The eight-week programme improved a shoulder stability test in 32 young elite players. In handball, another overhead sport, a trial in 660 elite players found that shoulder rotation, strength and mobility exercises three times a week in the warm-up lowered the risk of shoulder problems by 28%.

At the top level, volleyball has a low injury rate for a team sport. Data from 32 major international tournaments showed 3.8 time-loss injuries per 1,000 player hours of matches. The ankle accounted for 26% of injuries, the knee 15% and fingers or thumb 11%. The authors note this rate matches studies of lower levels of play.

One large Dutch trial gives a picture of injury rates in recreational adult play. Among 672 recreational players, the usual-warm-up group had 11.3 acute injuries per 1,000 hours, against 8.9 with a structured warm-up called VolleyVeilig. After adjustment the difference was no longer clear. Injury was counted differently from the elite data, so the two rates cannot be compared directly.

Blocking is a common source of finger injuries. In a Danish survey of 295 elite and recreational players, indoor injuries occurred mostly during blocking and spiking, with blocking leading to finger injuries. Among Danish elite players, fingers were the most common site of acute injury at 21%, and 28% of all injuries happened while blocking.

A typical finger injury happens when the ball strikes the fingertips at the block. World-level data suggest these injuries are undercounted, because players often tape the finger and keep playing. In Danish emergency department records, women had more hand and finger injuries than men, and the authors called for better blocking and overhand passing technique.

Casual volleyball counts as moderate activity and competitive indoor play as vigorous. The 2024 Compendium of Physical Activities, mostly built on measured values, rates casual team play at 3.0 METs, competitive indoor play at 6.0 and beach play at 8.0. One MET is the energy used sitting quietly. The CDC counts 3 to 5.9 METs as moderate and 6 or more as vigorous.

Much of a volleyball match is played at modest heart rates. In 24 senior female players in Turkey, average heart rate during a match was 117 beats a minute, and every player spent more than half of the match below 60% of her maximum. Liberos had the highest heart rates and setters the lowest.

Shorter breaks between rallies made the game a better workout in one small trial. In Serbia, 34 untrained men aged 25 to 55 played twice a week for 12 weeks. Both groups lowered their blood pressure, but only the group playing with shorter breaks improved body weight, BMI and a shuttle-run fitness test.

People who play team sports report fewer bad mental health days. In a survey of 1.2 million US adults, those who exercised reported 1.49 fewer poor mental health days a month than matched non-exercisers, and team sports showed the largest difference, at 22%. The survey was a snapshot, so it cannot show that the sport caused the difference.

Reviews of adult sport also link team play with better mental health. A 2023 review of 29 studies linked sport with better wellbeing, less depression, anxiety and stress, and a sense of belonging, with team sport showing more favourable results than individual sport. An earlier review credited the social side of club and team sport, while noting that most studies were cross-sectional.

Trials of team sport for mental health are few and mixed. A 2026 review found six studies with 744 adults, with inconsistent effects, and suggested the main value may be wellbeing and social connection. On sticking with exercise, the evidence is indirect: feeling good during exercise and doing it for its own sake are both linked to staying active.

Jump training raises jump height in healthy people. A meta-analysis of 26 studies found that plyometric training, meaning quick rebounding jumps, raised standing jump height by about 9%, and jump height with an arm swing by about 7.5%. On a 50 centimetre jump, 9% would be about 4.5 centimetres.

Jump training programmes of more than 10 weeks and 20 sessions gave the best chance of clear gains. A meta-analysis of 56 studies also found that mixing squat jumps, countermovement jumps and drop jumps beat using one type, and that adding weight brought no extra benefit. People with more sports experience improved more.

Volleyball players gain from jump training even with all the jumping they already do. Across 12 trials in 326 players, plyometric training alone improved jump height, and programme length made no clear difference. Another 2026 review found that splitting the same weekly jumps into more frequent sessions changed little, though certainty was low.

Lifting weights alone may not raise jump height quickly. In a Greek trial of 55 female players over eight weeks, weight training raised squat strength by 17 to 19% in every training group. Jump height improved clearly only in the groups that added drop jumps from a well-chosen height on top of the weights.
