bluf.text: Start at the weight you are now. Body weight was not linked to climbing overuse injuries.
Climb easy routes often before you climb hard ones. Intensity and bouldering are where injury risk rises.
Use an open hand where you can and save hard crimping.
Climb down when you can, and keep your ankles strong for the falls you do not choose.

paragraphs.text: Muscle-strengthening activity in general is linked to a 10 to 17% lower risk of early death and major disease, and the WHO recommends it regularly for all adults. None of these studies looked at climbing itself.
Climbing loads the pulling muscles and the grip, which volleyball does not train. This is a description of the sport, not a study finding.
Success in climbing depends heavily on hand and forearm strength and endurance, which improve with training.

Overuse injuries in climbers were linked to higher intensity, bouldering, weak grip or fingers, the crimp grip and previous injury. BMI and body weight were not linked. The studies were of low average quality.
In bouldering, falls mostly injure the legs: 67% of fall injuries in one survey were to the lower limb, most often an ankle sprain, and 85% of the falls were unplanned.
Balance training lowers ankle sprain risk by about 40% across sports, which matters for landing falls as much as for volleyball.
Expect your forearms to tire first. Hand and forearm strength and endurance are what the research rates as highly important for climbing.
Experienced climbers tend to be lean with large forearms. That describes people who have climbed for years. It is not an entry requirement.

sections.heading: What it asks and what it gives

paragraphs.text: Climbing works the heart as well as the arms. In a small study of 14 experienced climbers, indoor climbing raised heart rate to 74 to 85% of predicted maximum, with energy use similar to running at 8 to 11 minutes per mile.

Most climbing energy comes from steady aerobic work and from the fast system that powers efforts of a few seconds. In a study of 13 climbers, recreational climbers used about 60 kJ on an easy route that cost elite climbers about 40 kJ, so smooth technique saves effort.

Beginners gain grip strength from bouldering alone. In a Brazilian study, 27 newcomers who bouldered for 18 weeks improved grip strength, hang time and forearm blood flow more than 26 controls. A meta-analysis of 18 trials of climbing as therapy, in 568 patients, also found a significant physical benefit.

Bouldering combined with psychotherapy eased depression as much as standard group therapy in a German trial. Among 156 outpatients, 10 weeks of bouldering psychotherapy moved symptoms from moderate to mild, matched group cognitive behavioural therapy and kept its benefit for at least 12 months.

A second German trial found a benefit against usual care. In 128 adults, bouldering psychotherapy cut depression scores by 4.2 points more than treatment as usual, a moderate effect. Response rates were 29.7% with bouldering against 21.1% in the control group.

These results come from therapy groups, not casual climbing. A Swedish review of 7 studies with 471 people, all in Germany or Austria, called for trials that separate climbing from the therapy around it. Low mood lasting weeks calls for a doctor; climbing can add to treatment, not replace it.

Beginners and experienced climbers tend to get hurt in different ways. In interviews with 314 German indoor climbers, beginners mostly had skin injuries and leg sprains from falling. Experienced climbers more often hurt finger tendons and pulleys on small holds.

Serious acute injuries in climbing gyms are uncommon. A German gym logged 515,337 visits over five years and 30 acute injuries, 0.02 per 1,000 hours, with no deaths. A review of more than 400 injury studies ranked indoor climbing lowest of all sports assessed.

Minor injuries are common in bouldering when climbers report every one. In a 12-month study of 507 indoor boulderers who reported monthly, 44% had at least one injury, though 78% of the 305 injuries were the mildest grade. The two studies counted injuries differently, so their rates cannot be compared directly.

Risk tends to rise with experience, grade and hours. A survey of 1,962 sport climbers found 0.2 injuries per 1,000 hours, linked to years climbing, difficulty and weekly time. A review of 19 studies added lead climbing and high intensity as possible risk factors.

The pulleys are bands of tissue that hold the finger tendons to the bone. A 2026 review puts pulley injuries at up to 20% of climbing injuries, most notably from crimping, where the middle finger joint bends sharply. In a small study, the crimp loaded the main pulley with about three times the fingertip force.

Expert bodies advise beginners to leave intense finger training for later. The UIAA Medical Commission, part of the international climbing federation, reserves campus board training for climbers with about 8 to 10 years of experience. A Norwegian-led review says fingerboard training should be limited in lower-graded climbers. Both are expert opinion.

Hangboard trials so far have tested intermediate and advanced climbers, not beginners. In Norway, 35 such climbers gained 17% in peak finger force after 10 weeks of two weekly sessions. In Germany, 30 climbers on an 8-week weighted plan gained more grip strength than controls.

Whether finger training prevents injury is not known. In a survey of 745 recreational climbers, fingerboard users had higher odds of injury, though a survey cannot show the board caused it. A 2026 clinical review argues for hangboarding as prevention but says randomised trials are still needed.

The UIAA Medical Commission links many climbing overuse injuries to muscle imbalance. In its view, pulling muscles grow while the rotator cuff, the small muscles that steady the shoulder, and the forearm muscles that open the hand are neglected. It advises training the complementary muscles. This is expert opinion.

Climbers do show a shift in shoulder strength balance. In a Hong Kong study, 31 experienced sport climbers had weaker outward rotation compared with inward rotation than 27 non-climbers. The authors said its clinical meaning has yet to be examined.

One small trial tested a shoulder programme for climbers. Among 84 male student climbers in Ukraine, closed-chain exercises, where the hand pushes against a fixed surface, plus slow lowering and strength work went with fewer shoulder injuries, 0.5 against 3.2 per 1,000 exposures. One trial cannot settle the question.

Where climbers get hurt differs by sex. In an international survey of 1,513 climbers, half had an injury in the past year. Shoulders were the most common site in women and fingers in men, which the authors linked partly to training aims and climbing style.

Bouldering injuries that reach hospital are mostly to the legs. At a Munich trauma centre, 61% of injuries in 430 patients were to the lower limbs, most often the ankle. At a UK trauma centre, ankle fractures made up 40% of 176 cases after an average fall of 2.9 metres.

Jumping off the wall was linked to the more serious leg injuries in bouldering. In the German 12-month study, leg injuries were more severe and were tied to jumping off the wall and to falling. No preventive measure studied showed a clear protective effect, in line with an earlier US study.

Teaching falling technique and full mat cover are recommended, but untested. The German interview study blamed beginners’ falls partly on missing fall technique and gaps between crash mats, and called for instruction for beginners. No trial of fall training was found for this article.

Bouldering means short climbs over thick mats with no rope. In top roping the rope runs from an anchor above, so falls are short. In lead climbing the rope is clipped in on the way up, so falls are longer. This is plain description.

Each style carries its own pattern of risk. In the German gym study, 6 acute injuries happened while bouldering, 16 while lead climbing and 7 while top roping, and bouldering injuries were mostly falls onto the mat. A review of overuse injuries linked bouldering to higher overuse risk.

Warming up is sensible, but its power to prevent injury is not proven. A review of five good-quality trials across sports found three where a warm-up lowered injury risk and two where it did not. The authors judged that the weight of evidence favours a lower risk.

Short warm-ups prepare the shoulders, but not the fingers, for climbing. In a Taiwanese crossover study of 22 recreational climbers, three different 10-minute warm-ups all improved shoulder range of motion and stability and raised elbow and shoulder strength. None of them raised finger strength.

The UIAA Medical Commission advises a proper warm-up at the start of a session and stretching at the end, from elbow to fingertip, without overstretching single finger joints. A few easy climbs at the start is one simple way to warm the fingers.

Volleyball already loads the fingers, shoulders and ankles that climbing uses. In US emergency data on adult volleyball arm injuries, fingers made up 33% and shoulders 29%. Ankle sprains are the commonest acute volleyball injury, up to half of all injuries.

Spacing climbing away from volleyball nights is an inference, not a tested plan. Both sports load the fingers, shoulders and ankles, and injuries rose with weekly climbing hours in a Slovenian survey of 191 climbers. Climbing on other days, keeping early months easy and climbing down rather than jumping would limit the overlap.

bluf.text: Two sessions a week meets the guideline.
Start small. Fewer than three sets per exercise is enough for the first 12 weeks.
Lift on whichever days work. Packing your activity into one or two days is as good for long-term health as spreading it out.
While losing weight, keep lifting and eat protein at each meal to hold on to muscle.

paragraphs.text: For beginners, one weekly session with fewer than three sets per multi-joint exercise, at loads under half of your maximum, is enough to gain strength for at least the first 12 weeks. The source is a narrative review.
The largest reduction in risk of early death was seen at about 30 to 60 minutes of muscle-strengthening activity a week.
People who fit their weekly activity into one or two days had similar death rates to people who spread it out.
Resistance training does not enhance weight loss, though it may increase lean mass and fat loss.
In older adults with obesity, lifting while dieting prevented about 93% of the muscle loss that dieting alone caused.
In 24 weight-loss trials, higher-protein diets kept about 0.4 kg more lean mass and lost about 0.9 kg more fat than standard-protein diets.
Adults are advised to do muscle-strengthening activity on two days a week.
Light loads working at first is expected. The review above found beginners progress on loads below 50% of their maximum.

More weekly sets build more muscle, but each extra set adds less than the one before. A 2017 review of 15 studies linked each added weekly set with about 0.4% more muscle growth. A 2026 analysis of 67 studies found the same for size and strength, with sharper diminishing returns for strength.

The American College of Sports Medicine's 2026 position stand lists what most helps strength. Strength rose more with loads of at least 80% of maximum, full range of motion, two to three sets, placing the exercise early in a session and at least two sessions a week. Muscle growth was greater with ten or more sets a week.

Light weights build as much muscle as heavy ones when sets are taken to failure. A review of 21 studies, in which every set went until no more repetitions were possible, found similar muscle growth with light and heavy loads. Gains in maximum strength, measured as the heaviest weight lifted once, were larger with heavy loads.

Sets of more than 15 repetitions built as much muscle as heavy sets in a 2021 review of 28 studies. Muscle growth did not differ between low, moderate and high loads, all taken to failure. Strength gains were larger with moderate and high loads, and untrained people gained the most muscle.

Training to failure is not needed to gain strength or muscle. A review of 15 studies in young adults found no significant difference between failure and non-failure training for strength or muscle size. Training to failure did not seem to harm results either.

Finishing sets nearer to failure may matter a little more for muscle size than for strength. A 2023 review found only a trivial size advantage for sets taken to failure. A 2024 analysis estimated the repetitions left in reserve and found size rose as sets ended closer to failure, while strength was similar across a wide range.

The NHS gives a simple test of effort that needs no counting. It says strength exercises should be done to the point where a short rest is needed before repeating the activity. Ending sets once the movement is hard, with a few repetitions left, fits this and the trials above.

sections.heading: How often, and rest between sets

paragraphs.text: How many days a week a muscle is trained matters little once weekly sets are the same. A review of 25 studies found no meaningful difference in muscle growth between frequencies when volume was equal. A review of 22 studies found strength rose with more sessions, but not when volume was matched.

Resting a little over a minute between sets may build slightly more muscle than very short rests. A 2024 review of nine studies found a small benefit to rests longer than 60 seconds, perhaps because people then lift more in later sets. It found no clear extra gain from resting longer than 90 seconds.

sections.heading: Progress, at home or in a gym

paragraphs.text: Gradual progress is the core advice, while many popular details matter less. The 2026 position stand advises healthy adults to train progressively. It found that training to momentary fatigue, equipment type, exercise complexity, time under tension and periodisation, meaning planned changes across weeks, did not consistently change results.

Adding repetitions works about as well as adding weight. In a trial of 43 people with at least a year of leg training, one group added weight over time while the other kept the weight and added repetitions. After eight weeks, muscle growth and strength were similar.

Push-ups built chest muscle and pressing strength as well as a light bench press in a small Japanese trial. Eighteen young men trained twice a week for eight weeks, with push-ups adjusted, for example by kneeling, to match 40% of their bench press maximum. Both groups gained similar strength and chest and triceps muscle.

Elastic bands produced strength gains similar to weight machines and dumbbells. A review of eight studies found no advantage for either method in upper or lower body strength. The NHS lists bands, body weight exercises and heavy household tasks among ways to build strength at home or in a gym.

Muscle soreness after training is most common after a break or when an exercise is new. A review notes that lowering movements, called eccentric actions, cause more of the small muscle injuries involved, and that the cause of soreness is uncertain. Exercise eases it for a while, and lighter training for one to two days was advised.

Soreness usually drops the second time the same exercise is done. A review of 20 studies found more soreness and a larger strength dip after a first session than after a repeat. Stretching does little: a Cochrane review of 12 studies found it cut soreness by about one point on a 100-point scale.

Soreness is not a sign that a session built more muscle. In a study of ten young men, muscle damage was highest in the first week of training and was unrelated to later growth. Growth was linked with muscle building measured at weeks three and ten, after the damage had faded. Chasing soreness has no support here.

Weight-training sports appear to have relatively low injury rates compared with common team sports. A review of 20 studies found about 0.24 to 1 injury per 1,000 hours in bodybuilding and 4.5 to 7.5 in strongman and Highland Games. Only four of the studies followed athletes forward in time, which weakens the figures.

Many weight-training injuries seen in US emergency rooms came from dropped weights rather than the lift itself. Data from 1990 to 2007 estimated about 970,000 such injuries. Weights dropping on the person caused 65.5%, and 90.4% involved free weights. Careful handling of weights addresses the commonest cause.

Nordic nutrition advice puts adult protein needs at about 0.83 g per kg of body weight a day. The review behind it cites 1.2 to 2.0 g per kg for active people eating less than they burn, and 1.0 to 1.2 for healthy older adults. Protein comes from many animal and plant foods.

Extra protein gives training a modest boost that levels off. A review of 49 trials found added protein raised strength by about 2.5 kg on a one-repetition lift and lean mass by 0.3 kg. Gains stopped rising above a total intake of about 1.6 g per kg a day, and were smaller with age.

Strength training lowered sports injuries in randomised trials. A review of 25 trials with 26,610 people found that strength training cut injuries to less than a third of the usual rate. Exercise programmes overall almost halved overuse injuries, while stretching showed no clear benefit.

Combining lifting with other training does not blunt gains in muscle or maximal strength, but may blunt explosive strength. A review of 43 studies found explosive gains were smaller when both were done in the same session, but not when sessions were at least three hours apart. The other training was running or cycling, not court sport.

For jump height itself, jump training seems to matter more than lifting alone. A review of 12 studies in female soccer players found that plyometric training, meaning repeated jumps and bounds, improved vertical jump more than strength training did. In professional soccer, strength training had smaller effects during the season than before it.

The dose evidence comes mainly from young men. Participants in the 67 studies of the 2026 dose analysis averaged 25 years of age, and 79% were male. All 15 studies in the failure review were in young adults, and its authors call for more research in older and highly trained people.

Trials behind the 2026 position stand lasted 6 to 52 weeks, so they say little about years of lifting. Across 137 reviews with more than 30,000 people, few programme details changed the main results. How training choices play out over decades remains unknown.

bluf.text: Aim for more steps than you take now. Benefit keeps rising up to about 8,000 to 10,000 a day for adults under 60.
Do not treat 10,000 as a pass mark. Around 6,000 already carries much of the benefit.
Use short walks to break up long stretches of sitting.
On a low day, a walk is a legitimate tool for mood.
Use a step counter if you like having one. It helps a little.

paragraphs.text: In 15 cohorts with 47,471 adults, taking more steps was linked to a lower risk of death, levelling off at 8,000 to 10,000 steps a day for adults under 60 and 6,000 to 8,000 for those 60 and over. The authors note there is little evidence behind the 10,000 figure.
Compared with the least active quarter of people, who took about 3,600 steps a day, the next quarter at about 5,800 steps had a 40% lower risk of death.
A five-minute walk each hour raised energy and mood and lowered fatigue in a small trial of sedentary adults.
Walking or jogging was among the most effective forms of exercise for depression across 218 trials, with low confidence in the exact size of the effect.
Apps and activity trackers raise activity by about 1,850 steps a day on average across 28 trials.
In the cohorts above, the typical person in the middle of the range took between about 5,800 and 7,800 steps a day.
The WHO guideline says some physical activity is better than none.

A brisk walk is one where talking is easy but singing is not. The NHS puts brisk walking at about 3 miles an hour. In a lab study of 76 adults aged 21 to 40, about 100 steps a minute matched moderate intensity and 130 matched vigorous intensity. The NHS says even a brisk 10-minute daily walk counts towards weekly activity.

Walking faster is linked to lower risk of death. Among 50,225 walkers in British cohorts, people who called their pace average or brisk had 20% and 24% lower death rates than slow walkers. The link held for men and women alike and was clearest in people over 50. In UK Biobank, faster stepping was linked to lower disease risk beyond total steps.

Whether pace matters beyond step count is not settled. In 4,840 US adults, stepping intensity was not linked to death rates once total steps were accounted for. In 16,741 older women, intensity links mostly faded after adjusting for steps, and benefit levelled off at about 7,500 steps a day. Total walking appears to matter most, with pace a possible bonus.

A walk soon after a meal blunts the rise in blood sugar that follows it. A meta-analysis of eight small crossover trials with 116 people found exercise after eating lowered post-meal glucose more than exercise before eating or no exercise. The sooner after the meal, the larger the effect. The trials carried a high risk of bias.

Timing can matter as much as the total. In 41 adults with type 2 diabetes, 10 minutes of walking after each main meal lowered post-meal blood sugar more than one 30-minute walk a day, most of all after the evening meal. In inactive young women, walks after meals lowered post-meal glucose but did not change the 24-hour average.

Enough daily activity appears to cancel out the risk linked to sitting. In data from more than a million people, about 60 to 75 minutes a day of moderate activity seemed to eliminate the higher death risk tied to long sitting, though not fully for TV viewing. In 44,370 people wearing activity monitors, 30 to 40 minutes a day weakened the link.

Short walking breaks during a long sit lower blood sugar and insulin after meals. A meta-analysis of seven one-day trials, mostly in adults with overweight, found light walking breaks beat continued sitting on both measures. Walking breaks also beat standing breaks. These were single-day studies, so long-term effects are unknown.

Japan's 2023 national guide sets walking as the everyday benchmark. It recommends at least 60 minutes a day of walking or similar activity for adults, about 8,000 steps, and about 6,000 steps for older adults. It also says breaking up long sitting, for example every 30 minutes, matters for heart and metabolic health.

Walking eases symptoms of depression and anxiety. A meta-analysis of 75 trials with 8,636 people found walking reduced both compared with doing nothing, whether indoors or outdoors, alone or in a group. Walking did about as well as other active comparisons. People who were already depressed showed larger improvements.

A walk may help when stuck on a problem. In four experiments, walking raised scores on a test of generating ideas for 81% of participants, and the boost lasted for a while after sitting back down. It did little for tests with one right answer. These were short experiments with creativity tests, not studies of daily life.

More daily steps go with lower risk of dementia and depression over time. A 2025 meta-analysis of 57 studies found 7,000 steps a day, against 2,000, linked to 38% lower dementia risk and 22% lower risk of depressive symptoms. Only two or three studies fed each estimate, and these cohorts cannot prove cause.

Walking alone moves the scale only a little. A meta-analysis of nine step-counter walking programmes with 307 people and no diet change found an average loss of about 1.3 kg (3 lb), or 0.05 kg a week. Longer programmes led to more loss. Walking is a weak tool for weight loss on its own.

Walking improves health markers that the scale does not show. Across 32 trial reports in inactive adults, walking raised fitness and lowered blood pressure, waist size and body fat, along with a small weight loss of about 1.4 kg. It did not change blood fats. Judging a walking habit by weight alone misses much of its value.

Regular walking helped keep low back pain from coming back in a large trial. In Australia, 701 adults who had recently recovered from back pain were split into a walking and education programme or no treatment. The walking group went a median 208 days before a flare-up, against 112. Across five trials, walking eased chronic back pain as well as other exercise.

Walking does not appear to wear out arthritic knees. Among 1,212 people aged 50 and over with knee arthritis, those who walked for exercise were less likely to develop frequent knee pain. A review of 18 studies found walking programmes made little or no difference to measures of load on the knee joint, while walking speed rose slightly.

With a sore back, the NHS advises staying active and keeping up daily activities, and lists walking among activities that may help. It advises seeing a GP if pain has not improved after a few weeks or stops daily activities. Back pain with fever, or with numbness or weakness in both legs, needs urgent help.

Watches count steps fairly well, but their calorie numbers are unreliable. A review of 158 studies found that major brands measured steps accurately in the lab, but none measured energy burned accurately. A second review found step errors under 25% for one common tracker, and energy errors above 30% for every brand.

A phone only counts the steps it is carried for. In a Japanese study of 54 adults over a week, iPhones recorded 12% fewer steps than a pedometer worn on the waist. The gap was largest in people who seldom carried their phone. A phone total is best read as a rough floor.

Walking with other people has been tested and appears to help. A review of 42 studies with 1,843 people in outdoor walking groups found lower blood pressure, resting heart rate and body fat, and fewer symptoms of depression, with no notable side effects. In a UK survey, dog owners had four times the odds of meeting activity guidelines.

Walking as transport and a few active days both count. Among 263,450 UK adults, walking to work was linked to lower risk of heart disease, though not lower death from all causes. In 3,101 US adults, reaching 8,000 steps on just one or two days a week was linked to lower death rates than never reaching it.

Walking in nature seems to lift mood more than walking along streets. A meta-analysis of experiments found natural settings beat urban ones for anxiety, fatigue and vigour. In one study, a 90-minute walk in a natural area reduced brooding thoughts and activity in a related brain region, while the same walk in a city did not.

Whether outdoor walking beats indoor walking is less clear. Early trials found more energy and enjoyment after exercise in nature than the same exercise indoors, but most were single sessions in students. A 2019 review of 28 trials found limited evidence of extra benefit, and quality was low. Any walk counts, and a green route is a pleasant extra.
